TESTIMONY OF THE
DEPARTMENT OF INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON INLAND FISHERIES AND
WILDLIFE
IN OPPOSITION TO L.D. 205
"AN ACT TO AMEND THE BAG LIMIT FOR TURKEY"
SPONSORED BY: Senator TIMBERLAKE of Androscoggin
CO-SPONSORED BY: Senator BLACK of Franklin and
V
Representative LYMAN of Livermore Falls, Representative WOOD of Greene
DATE OF HEARING: Wednesday, February 12, 2025 Good afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee. I am Bob Cordes, Special Projects Biologist at the
Department of lnland Fisheries and Wildlife, speaking on behalf of the Department, in
opposition to L.D. 205.
This bill provides that bag limits for wild turkey established by rule by the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife must be the same as bag limits for ruffed grouse.
While we appreciate the intent of this bill and the desire to simplify hunting regulations,
aligning bag limits for turkey and grouse would potentially threaten the sustainability of our wild turkey population, or significantly reduce hunting opportunities for ruffed
grouse, wild turkey, or both species. Although wild turkey and ruffed grouse are game birds, they are distinct species with unique life history traits, management
considerations, habitat needs, and social tolerance. The wild turkey has a limited distribution in Maine due to habitat availability and impacts of severe winter conditions that occur in northern, western and eastern Maine. Turkey populations can be
impacted by overharvest, particularly when females are harvested in the fall. In
contrast, the ruffed grouse has a robust statewide population, with population levels
primarily driven by spring and summer weather, which can affect young-of-the-year survival. Unlike with turkeys, hunting mortality has been shown to have very little
influence over grouse numbers, even in marginal habitats. The Department recently went through an extensive planning process to develop wild turkey management, goals and objectives. This process included multiple opportunities for public input, including a scientific survey of public attitudes towards wild turkeys.

That effort identified several wildlife managements districts (WM Ds) that were
approaching or exceeding social tolerance and in need of population stabilization. To address this issue, in 2019 the Department established a season framework with
liberalized fall bag limits in those specific WMDs to stabilize populations through the harvest of females. However, in many northern WMDs the wild turkey population is
small and very vulnerable to overharvest.
Currently, total bag limits for wild turkey in the fall range from 1 to 5 turkeys, with
several WMDs closed to fall hunting completely. Bag limits for ruffed grouse are set at 4
per day, statewide. If the Department was required to implement this bill, we would
have to either increase the bag limit of wild turkey to match those of ruffed grouse, reduce the bag limit of ruffed grouse to match those of wild turkey, close hunting
seasons for one or both species in some WMDs, or adjust the bag limits for both species
to align them with each other. Since the Department is statutorily mandated to ensure the sustainability of all our native wildlife species, one option would be to propose a
significant reduction to bag limits for ruffed grouse, and possibly even close grouse
hunting seasons in some WMDs, to prevent population declines or local extirpation of
wild turkeys. This would undoubtedly be very upsetting to tens of thousands of hunters
that enjoy hunting ruffed grouse. Alternatively, we could propose a significant
reduction in the length of the wild turkey season, to prevent the overharvest that would otherwise occur by increasing the bag limit to match ruffed grouse. Again, this approach would likely be met with significant resistance from wild turkey hunters.
Alternatively, the Department could increase bag limits for turkeys to match those of
ruffed grouse and accept that overharvest may result in significant population declines in some WMDs. However, this approach would be in conflict with the goals ofthe publicly derived Turkey Management Plan and would likely reduce or eliminate opportunities for spring turkey hunting in some WMDs.
I would be glad to answer any questions at this time or during the work session.

Testimony in Opposition to LD 205 An Act to Amend the Bag Limit for Turkey
February 12, 2025 Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts, and members of the committee, my name is James Cote and I here today on behalf of the Maine Professional Guides Association in respectful opposition to LD 205. MPGA represents numerous professional guides that offer turkey hunting opportunities for their clients. We absolutely recognize and acknowledge many of the concerns you will hear from Senator Timberlake as his reasons for bringing this legislation forward. However, we are concerned about the potential impact that a bag limit of four turkeys per day, the same as ruffed grouse, would have on Maine's turkey population. While we don't have a perfect solution for the nuisance turkey issues that some landowners experience, we do believe that increasing hunting opportunities (seasons, bag limits, etc...) in reasonable ways that are supported by the Department's historical biological research may be a more sustainable and advantageous way to lower the population, especially in distinct areas and land-bases where turkey populations are most detrimental. We also wonder if more should be done with depredation-like permits that allow certain landowners (farmers) to engage in more aggressive management of local turkey populations in more cost-effective and less time-intensive ways. Thank you for your consideration and I would be pleased to answer any questions or follow up with additional information as requested.
An organization of professional guides dedicated to promoting a quality, ethical outdoor experience.

Joint Standing Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife on LD 205 "An Act to
Amend the Bag Limit for Turkey" Public Hearing: March 12, 2025

Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and members of the joint standing committee on
Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, I am Senator Jeff Timberlake and I am here to present LD 205, "An Act to Amend the Bag Limit for Turkey" and ask for your support.
I have put this bill forward due to the significant increase in Maine's wild turkey population in recent years, which has been driven in part by the fact that turkeys can hatch up to three times per year. While the reintroduction efforts from the late 1970s have been a success, the
turkey population has now grown beyond what local communities and the environment can
sustainably support.

Overpopulation is causing serious issues, particularly for our farmers. Crops such as strawberries, pumpkins, apples, and even tree buds are being damaged by wild turkeys, disrupting both agriculture and the natural balance of our ecosystem.

Because wild turkeys can hatch multiple times each year, their population is expanding at a
rate that the environment and local communities can't keep up with. In response, we need to
consider opening up the hunting season and increasing hunting opportunities to help manage their numbers.

I am proposing that we align the wild turkey bag limit with the partridge bag limit, as this approach has proven effective in managing the partridge population. By giving hunters a greater opportunity to help control turkey numbers, we can reduce crop damage and protect
Maine's agricultural landscape.

The partridge bag limit has been a successful model for population control, and applying a similar strategy to turkeys will help maintain a healthy balance between farming and
wildlife.

I urge the committee to support this legislation. Thank you for your time and consideration.
I am happy to answer any questions.

Re: LD 205: An Act to Amend the Bag Limit for Turkeys
Dear Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts, and Members of the Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
I am John Simoneau, Resident of Durham, submitting this testimony on behalf of New England Chapter of Backcountry Hunters & Anglers (BHA).
BHA seeks to ensure North America's outdoor heritage of hunting and fishing in a natural setting by supporting land conservation, public access to hunting and fishing areas, fair chase, and the sound management of fish and wildlife and their habitats.
On behalf of BHA's Maine members we are testifying in opposition of LD 205 An Act to Amend the Bag Limit for Turkeys. Consistent with our support for the North American Model of Wildlife Conservation, Backcountry Hunters & Anglers believes fish and wild resources belong to the public and supports science-based fish and wildlife management. BHA supports the authority and responsibility of state wildlife agencies to manage resident fish and wildlife populations.
In 2016 Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (MIFW) initiated an update to the Maine's Big Game Managment Plan. This update had a steering committee to guide the process and subcommittees to provide recommendations for the management of each big game species. The process included a public survey seeking input from residents, hunters and landowners. The Wild Turkey subcommittee included hunters, guides and landowners. This plan established the following management goals and objectives related to Wild Turkey.
Goal #1: Maintain a healthy, sustainable turkey population that provide opportunities for hunting and viewing, while also allowing turkeys to continue expanding into portions of northern, eastern, and western Maine.
Goal #2: Ensure public satisfaction with the turkey population
Goal #3: Increase the recreational value of the wild turkey resource by promoting participation in wild turkey hunting
Goal #4: Provide education to Maine residents (including hunters) on turkey biological, ecology, and management

These goals relate to the current spring seasonal turkey bag limits allowing for 1 bearded wild turkey in WMDS 1-6 & 8, but two bearded wild turkeys in WMDs 7, 9-29. The fall turkey hunt seasonal bag limit varies from 5 to 1 wild turkeys in the WMDs open, yet the season is closed in WMDs 1-5 & 9. This demonstrates that the Department is setting bag limits to match the objectives in the Big Game Management plan. This legislation as written sets the wild turkey bag limit the same as the ruffed grouse bag limit. The management framework for upland game (ruffed grouse) is different than for big game (wild turkey). As stated earlier the turkey bag limits are seasonal, like other big game such as deer, bear & moose. For upland game the limit is a Daily Bag and a Possession Limit, such that for ruffed grouse the limit is 4 daily and 8 in possession. These limits applied to wild turkey would not be in alignment with the Wild Turkey management plan objectives. In sum, we oppose LD 205: An Act to Amend the Bag Limit for Turkeys. It is important that the department continues to have the authority to set bag limits for turkey by rule. This rule making should be executed to meet the management goals and objectives in the Big Game management plan, which we believe the department is doing. To: The Honorable Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts, members of the.lnland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee From: Kevin Antonovitch, Solon, Maine Date: February 12, 2025
RE: Opposition to LD 205, An Act to Amend the Bag limit for Turkey
By way of background, I have been an outdoor enthusiast, consen/ationist and avid hunter for over four decades. About half way through my hunting career, I was introduced to Turkey
Hunting by a friend. That first skeptical introduction to the sport of Turkey Hunting has turned
into a passion which has become a strong part of my life. I am a Silver Life Sponsor member of the National Wild Turkey Federation, a Maine Certified Hunter Education Instructor, a member
of the Skowhegan Sportsmans Club and I have mentored many young and new hunters through
lecture, instruction and mentored hunts.
I believe that by allowing LD 205 to move fon/vard, would be detrimental to our current wild
turkey population, hunting opportunities and would further erode our hunting heritage which is
so entangled in our Maine way of life.
There are many reasons why LD 205 should not move forward. But l would like to bring a few
important reasons to your attention during the short time l have to speak.
LD 205, as proposed, does not address the sex of the birds han/ested or during which season those birds could be harvested. Wild turkeys breed and have their young in the spring of the year as do ruffed grouse. However, Ruffed grouse are hunted only in the fall after they have raised their young. Wild turkeys travel in flocks, ruffed grouse do not. There are currently two Wild Turkey seasons; a Spring and Fall season. Only males or "toms" are allowed to be harvested during the Spring season because the females or "hens" have been bred and are nesting. If LD 205 were moved fon/vard, it would allow four (4) either sex turkeys to be taken daily with up to eight (8) in possession during the spring hunt which currently only allows the han/esting of two (2) bearded birds. The harvesting of hens during the spring season would have an incredible impact on the current and future population of wild turkeys.
Turkey hunting, for those who have not participated in the sport, is addictive, exciting and interactive. Those three qualities make it very easy to introduce youth or new hunters to the sport of hunting. Turkey hunting takes place typically in the spring or early fall when it is an enjoyable and beautiful time to be outdoors. Maine's turkey seasons are some of the longest and allow ample opportunity. Those qualities of turkey hunting make it instrumental in maintaining and fostering our hunting heritage. lf LD 205 were moved forward, it would have a detrimental impact on our current turkey population and eventually impact how we introduce, retain, and bring back hunters whose numbers are nationally on the decline. Introducing new

hunters to turkey hunting could spark them to try other methods and species to hunt which in turn could bring revenue to the State.
lt seems like LD 205 is a knee jerk reaction to what seems like, to some, as an overabundance of turkeys or nuisance turkeys on the landscape. There are currently methods used by lF&W to
address those situations which are based on science and not passion. Those practices should be allowed to monitor and control those incidents. Currently, nuisance or overpopulation of
turkeys are controlled by depredation permits issued by lF&W or by trap and transport programs
which deal with those incidents.
l would like to suggest another solution to the over abundance problem, which would be
beneficial to both the hunter and those experiencing problems with wild turkeys. A website could be developed through lF&W where individuals who want to hunt turkeys could get in
contact with those farmers or individuals with an overabundance or nuisance wild turkey problem. in combination with the depredation permits, hunters could enjoy the hunt and harvest the birds. There are methods already in place or could be adopted to address nuisance or overpopulation of wild turkeys in specific areas. These methods should be utilized instead of negatively impacting the wild turkey population and its presence on the landscape.
By changing the bag limits on Wild Turkeys to reflect those limits on Ruffed Grouse there would be a significant negative impact on the Wild Turkey population and our hunting heritage. There are already means in place to deal with nuisance or over populations of Wild Turkeys and those programs should be allowed to remain and control those problems. The Department of lnland Fisheries and Wildlife was given the authority by the legislature to monitor and control the Wild Turkey population and other species through various seasons and bag limits that are
scientifically based. lF&W should be allowed to continue that mission.
Thank you for considering my testimony in opposition to LD 205 for the reasons I have stated.
Respectfully submitted,

Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and members of the committee for Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, my name is Tyler Brown and I submit the following testimony in opposition to LD 205 "An act to amend the bag limit for turkey"
Maine's turkey population has not always been one of abundance that is being seen in the lower half of the state, and is not consistent throughout the state. Beginning in 1942, the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife had begun reintroduction of wild turkeys since their expatriation due to over-hunting and habitat loss in the 1880s. Several attempts were made with no success, it was not until 1977 that the department successfully reintroduced (41) wild turkeys in York and Eliot. Five years later (33) turkey were trapped from the flourishing York county population and released into Waldo County.  Eight years after their successful re-introduction, the commissioner MEDIFW was given the authority to establish the first spring turkey season and in May of 1986, York county held its first Spring Turkey hunting season, held for (16) half-days, only allowing the hunt until noon, with permits allotted by lottery allowing the harvest of one bird. Six years later the season was expanded to include portions of Cumberland county, then in 1996 the zones were expanded to other counties and increased the permits from (750) to (1250). Six years later MEDIFW added the fall season and eliminated the permit lottery, then opening the opportunity for all hunters in 2005. The expansion of wild turkey hunting in all of Maine was not complete until 2014 when the Spring season was opened all day and in 2015 when all of Maine's Wildlife Management Districts had at least one season, thirty-eight years after their reintroduction.  Maine's current seasons are not uniform across the state, while the spring season allows for the taking of two male turkeys in the majority of WMD's, many of those in the north only allow the taking of one. The fall season is allowed in the majority of WMD's but not in (6) northern zones due to a lack of significant population. These unique situations require carefully crafted bag limits and season lengths based on the 6th Pillar of the North American Model for Wildlife Conservation "Science is the proper tool for discharge of wildlife policy".  Under Maines Revised Statute, Title 12, Part 13, Subpart 4, Chapter 915, Subchapter 8, Article 1, Subsection 11701, the authority to determine bag limits and season lengths rests with the Commissioner of MEDIFW "The commissioner may establish open seasons for hunting wild turkeys, designate areas that are open to the taking of wild turkeys in any part of the State, prescribe the form and regulate the number of permits to be issued, determine the number and sex of the birds to be harvested, establish bag limits, establish permit eligibility requirements, establish legal hunting times, specify the types of weapons to be used during any open wild turkey hunting season and make any other rules that the commissioner considers necessary for the protection of the wild turkey resource".

While Maine's turkey population may appear to be over-abundant to some, that is hardly the case for the entire state as evidenced by the varying seasons, nor is it the norm across our country. Many states in the south where wild turkeys were never expatriated, are experiencing serious declines in their turkey populations, Alabama, Georgia, Arkansas, Louisiana and Oklahoma have experienced sharp declines by as much as 18% with harvest rates declining by as much as 31% between 2014 and 2019.. Setting the bag limit in Maine law to the same as ruffed grouse allowing the take of (4) turkeys a day and up to (8) in one's possession, fails to account for the varying seasons and bag limits across our state and would not allow MEDIFW the ability to alter bag limits to account for declining populations in a timely manner to ensure a sustainable harvest and populations.  The successful reintroduction of wild turkeys after nearly a century since their expatriation is a testament to the success of the North American Model for Wildlife Conservation, and to the effective management of our wildlife by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife. Their science based methods and history of success in managing wild turkeys, is evidence that MEDIFW is the most qualified department to make responsible decisions based in science when regulating bag limits and season lengths to ensure sustainable wildlife populations for generations to come.  I urge you all to unanimously vote "Ought not to pass" on LD205 to preserve MEDIFW's ability to effectively manage our wildlife.  Thank you very much for your time and service to our state.  Tyler Brown
